analysis.one_liner: Lets homeowners facing foreclosure cut their mortgage balance in bankruptcy, and permanently raises deposit insurance.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on this foreclosure-relief bill: it was introduced and placed on the calendar in April 2009, sat there with no floor action, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let homeowners in Chapter 13 bankruptcy reduce what they owe on an underwater home to the home's current value, cap interest and fees, and stop foreclosure while a court-approved plan is paid off. It paired that with help for veterans and FHA and rural borrowers whose loans are modified, a liability shield for loan servicers who modify loans, a permanent increase in deposit insurance to $250,000, and a new Justice Department task force on mortgage fraud. It also trimmed the Treasury's bailout authority to offset the cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who are underwater on their mortgages and facing foreclosure, especially those in Chapter 13 bankruptcy, who could keep their homes on rewritten loan terms instead of losing them. Veterans, FHA borrowers, and rural borrowers also gain because their agencies would reimburse lenders when a bankruptcy court modifies a loan, making lenders more willing to modify. Bank depositors gain from the permanent $250,000 deposit insurance cap.

how_it_helps.text: Bankruptcy courts could reduce a mortgage balance to the home's fair market value for loans facing foreclosure, and stretch repayment up to 40 years at a market-based rate [S2][S3].

Debtors would not be liable for servicer fees and charges racked up during bankruptcy unless the servicer timely filed notice and the fees were lawful, reasonable, and covered by equity; prepayment penalties could be waived [S3].
A borrower whose loan may be foreclosed could satisfy the credit counseling requirement within 30 days after filing, instead of the 180 days beforehand the law normally requires [S2].

HUD could pay FHA insurance benefits on mortgages modified in bankruptcy and run a loan-modification program, the VA and USDA could reimburse holders of guaranteed loans modified in bankruptcy, and the HOPE for Homeowners program would be reworked to reach more borrowers [S2][S3].
Loan servicers would be shielded from liability and from investor contract claims when they modify loans in the borrower's interest, removing a legal excuse for not modifying [S2][S3].
Federal deposit insurance would rise permanently from $100,000 to $250,000, FDIC borrowing authority would rise from $30 billion to $100 billion, and NCUA's from $100 million to $6 billion [S2][S3].
A Nationwide Mortgage Fraud Task Force would be established in the Justice Department with branches in the ten states with the most mortgage fraud [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and investors in mortgage-backed securities would absorb the loss when courts write down loan balances, and servicers would lose fee income and face claims disallowed for Truth in Lending violations. The cost of reimbursing lenders on modified FHA, VA, and rural loans would be offset by a $2.3 billion cut to the Treasury's bailout authority. Future borrowers could face somewhat higher mortgage rates if lenders price in the risk of court-ordered write-downs.

drawbacks.text: Lenders and securitization investors argued that letting judges cut principal on primary residences would raise risk on home loans, tightening credit or raising rates for all future borrowers [S3].
The safe harbor would shield servicers from lawsuits by investors over loan modifications, including where the modification was not in investors' interest, weakening investor contract rights [S3].
Taxpayer-backed insurance payments to FHA, VA, and rural lenders after bankruptcy modifications shift part of the cost of keeping homes off lenders and onto government insurance funds [S2][S3].
The measure is heavily drawn to loans facing foreclosure and requires borrowers to first seek a modification outside bankruptcy, which could still leave lenders with delay and litigation costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: In the depths of the 2009 foreclosure wave, letting bankruptcy judges rewrite underwater mortgages was the strongest tool Congress considered for keeping people in their homes, and the bill cushioned lenders with government insurance payments and servicer liability shields to reduce the blow. The real cost falls on mortgage investors and, indirectly, on future borrowers through higher rates. The bill also carried a grab bag of unrelated items — deposit insurance, TARP authority, fraud enforcement — that made it a broader stabilization package than its title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: Dodd introduced it in late April 2009 and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but no vote was ever scheduled, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Dodd introduced the bill on April 24, 2009, with Durbin and Schumer [S1][S5].
Two days later it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 51, meaning it was waiting for floor consideration [S5][S3].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a vote or a committee markup, and it expired at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors in mortgage-backed securities are better off, because the authority to write down loan balances in bankruptcy never became law — the Senate had already defeated the same provision as an amendment to a companion housing bill by 45 to 51 on April 30, 2009, and this bill then sat unvoted on the calendar.

for.name: Sen. Chris Dodd
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it placed on the Senate calendar; never got it to a floor vote.

for.name: Sens. Dick Durbin and Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsors.

against.name: 39 of 42 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Helped defeat the identical bankruptcy mortgage-modification provision 45-51 when it was offered as an amendment to a companion housing bill on April 30, 2009, and no floor action followed on this bill.

against.name: 12 of 56 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Joined Republicans in voting down the bankruptcy mortgage-modification amendment on April 30, 2009.

against.name: Mortgage lenders and servicers, led by the Mortgage Bankers Association
against.what_they_did: Ran a major lobbying campaign against letting bankruptcy courts write down mortgage principal.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held on this bill; the identical bankruptcy write-down provision lost 45-51 on April 30, 2009, with Republicans almost uniformly opposed and a dozen Democrats joining them.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and holders of mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: Courts could cut loan balances to the home's current value for loans facing foreclosure, cap interest, and disallow fees and claims tainted by Truth in Lending violations. Lenders and securitization investors would absorb those losses directly, which is why they fought the provision.

The bill shields servicers from liability and investor contract claims when they modify loans, and lets HOPE for Homeowners pay servicers up to $1,000 per modified loan — but it also waives their unpaid fees in bankruptcy and disallows claims tied to lending-law violations.

Permanent $250,000 deposit insurance plus sharply higher FDIC and NCUA borrowing authority stabilize insured institutions, funded partly by industry special assessments. Depositors, not just banks, are the direct beneficiaries.

The bill tightens who can originate FHA loans, barring firms or staff with fraud convictions, debarments, or unresolved audit findings, and expands compliance reviews. Honest lenders gain a cleaner field; bad actors are shut out.

industries.industry: Government mortgage insurers (FHA, VA, USDA rural housing)
industries.note: The bill makes these agencies the payer of last resort when bankruptcy courts modify guaranteed or insured loans, locking in the government's role in backstopping home loans while making lenders willing to modify.
